title: Camp 3 close: a rule of life
hookLine: monks and Methodists alike write a simple rule: what I'll do daily, weekly, yearly

cards: This camp started with a simple question: what is prayer? Since then you've met a lot of practices. The Jesus Prayer and the psalter.
Lectio divina and the examen. Lament and dryness. Advent, Lent and Pascha.
The sabbath. The canon and translation. The tithe, alms and hospitality.
The hymn and the spiritual. Koinonia, fasting and testimony. The sacraments and the rosary.

teach.b: The word rule comes from the Latin regula, which first meant a straight stick, a ruler, something to keep a line from wandering. A rule of life isn't a list of prohibitions.

It's a simple, honest plan for what you'll actually do: daily, weekly, yearly. Take the Rule of Saint Benedict, written for monks in Italy. It covers prayer, work, meals, sleep, guests, even how much wine is allowed.

teach.h: BENEDICT: A LITTLE RULE FOR BEGINNERS.
teach.b: Near its end, Benedict calls it a little rule for beginners, and monks and nuns still live by it.
A popular motto, pray and work, is often pinned on Benedict, though it doesn't appear in the rule itself; it does sum up its rhythm.

teach.h: WESLEY: NO HARM, DO GOOD, PRACTICE.
teach.b: Much later, John Wesley wrote the General Rules for the Methodists, and they fit on a page: do no harm, do good, and keep the practices of the church, like prayer, scripture, the Lord's Supper and fasting.
Today many Christians, Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and evangelical, write their own short rule. Something like: daily, ten minutes of prayer and a psalm. Weekly, church and a sabbath afternoon.
Monthly, a fast day. Yearly, a retreat.
The secret of a good rule is that it's small enough to keep.
A rule you'll really follow beats a grand one you'll abandon by Thursday. A trellis in a garden doesn't make the vine grow. It gives it something to climb.
Tomorrow, camp four begins: the text itself, read in order, starting with the Gospel of Mark.

how: Monks and nuns live by a written rule such as the Rule of Saint Benedict, early Methodists kept Wesley's General Rules, and many Christians today write a short personal rule of daily, weekly and yearly practices, often with a spiritual director.

o: a straight stick, a ruler: the root of a rule of life
a list of things a monk is forbidden ever to do
an official decree from a Roman emperor or king

games.q: who wrote which rule — tap the pairs.

games.q: you're writing your first rule of life. you're full of enthusiasm. what does long experience suggest?
o: an hour of prayer a day, starting tomorrow.
something small enough to keep: a few minutes daily.
no plan: wait until you feel like it.
games.why: Benedict called his a little rule for beginners. a rule you'll actually follow beats a grand one you'll drop by Thursday.

practice: Look back over this camp and ask which one or two practices actually stuck, or quietly called to you.
Then write three lines, smaller than you think they should be, with no guilt and no grand vows: daily, one thing of five minutes or less; weekly, one thing; yearly, one thing.
If you pray, offer your three lines to God; if you don't, keep them somewhere you'll see them.

wordCard.voice: Regula, Latin for a straight stick, a ruler: the root of rule of life, a short plan that keeps you from wandering.

orig.note: Latin: a straight stick, a ruler — and so a rule, a pattern of life.

carryVoice: Your line: small rules keep big loves. Camp three is done. That's day one hundred fifty-six.
